screens.title: Caching Strategies: Design and Implementation
screens.narratorSegment: Caching is a practical, high-impact technique that reduces latency and lightens the load on databases. In real systems we place caches at multiple layers — in the client, at CDNs for static assets, in proxy layers, inside application processes, or as a distributed cache like Redis that many servers share. During this lesson you will learn the three core strategies — Cache-Aside, Write-Through, and Write-Back — and why each fits different read/write patterns. You will also learn how invalidation, TTL, and eviction policies like LRU change behavior under load. Concrete examples include using Cache-Aside for read-heavy content such as trending articles, and choosing Write-Back for very high write throughput where occasional data loss is tolerable. We will also discuss operational risks: stale data, over-caching, cache stampedes, and how to avoid single points of failure. By the end you will be able to pick a strategy, explain its trade-offs, and sketch a simple Cache-Aside implementation that uses a dictionary to simulate Redis. Think about a feature you recently used that felt slow — caching is often the fastest path to making that interaction feel instant.

screens.title: What is caching and why it matters
screens.narratorSegment: Caching is the practice of storing copies of data in a faster, temporary layer that sits between an application and its primary data store. The main goals are to reduce latency for frequent requests and to offload the database so the system can serve more traffic. A clear example is a user profile service: rather than hitting the slow database for every profile view, a cache stores the profile so subsequent reads are immediate. This reduces response time and decreases the number of expensive database queries. A common misconception is that caches are only for reads: while reads benefit most, writes are also important because they create stale cache entries unless invalidated. Another misconception is that caching always saves money; over-caching can increase memory costs and operational complexity without proportional benefit. Practically, you should cache only data with high access frequency or high cost to compute. When designing a cache, consider where it lives — client, CDN, proxy, in-process, or distributed — because placement affects latency, hit rate, and complexity. A good design balances speed, cost, and correctness: choose what to cache, how to invalidate it, and how to evict items when memory is full. Reflect: which part of your system would benefit most from a cache and why?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.6 › What is caching
Core Concept

Caching: definition and purpose

Caching stores copies of data in a faster layer to reduce latency and database load. It brings frequently-requested data closer to the consumer.

Primary goals
  • Reduce request latency
  • Offload the primary database
Real-world example
User profiles cached to avoid repeated slow database reads for every page view.
Key Takeaway

Cache where it provides meaningful latency or cost savings, and pair it with invalidation and eviction policies.

Placement
Client-side
Browser and mobile caches reduce network hops for UI assets and small responses.
CDN & Proxy
Static assets cached geographically closer to users; proxies cache responses at the edge.
Application & Distributed
In-process caches for microsecond access; Redis or Memcached for shared, in-memory storage across servers.
Misconception check: Caching is not a free performance win. Measure hit rates and understand when caching adds operational cost without benefit.

screens.title: Cache placements in system architecture
screens.narratorSegment: Caches appear at many levels in a system and each placement changes the trade-offs you face. Client-side caches reduce network traffic and accelerate UI interactions but are limited in size and consistency control. CDNs cache static assets like images and scripts close to users and offer strong latency benefits for geographically distributed traffic. Proxy caches can store HTTP responses at intermediate layers, reducing load on origin servers. Application-level caches live inside the server process and provide ultra-low latency, but they are local to a single instance and not shared. Distributed caches, such as Redis or Memcached, provide a shared in-memory key-value store accessible by many application servers and are the most common in backend system design; they balance speed and shareability but require careful replication and availability planning. Databases may also expose internal caches. Choosing placement depends on access locality, consistency needs, and operational constraints. For example, session state might be stored in a distributed cache to allow horizontal scaling of app servers, while static site assets belong on a CDN. A common mistake is assuming a single cache layer solves all problems — in reality you often combine several placements to meet latency and consistency goals.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.6 › Cache placements
Placement

Where to put a cache

Client-side
Fast UI interactions; limited control and size.
CDN
Best for static assets and geographic proximity.
Proxy
Caches HTTP responses at the network edge or in front of origin servers.
Distributed & App
Application-level caches live inside a process for microsecond access; distributed caches such as Redis or Memcached provide shared access across processes and servers.
Use case: sessions
Store session state in a distributed cache to allow any app server to serve user requests.
Use case: hot data
Cache hot or frequently-read rows in Redis for rapid access in read-heavy services.
Common mistake: pick placement by convenience rather than access pattern; that leads to suboptimal hit rates or consistency gaps.

screens.title: Cache-Aside (Lazy Loading)
screens.narratorSegment: Cache-Aside, also called lazy loading, is a straightforward pattern where the application checks the cache before going to the database. On a hit, the cached data is returned immediately. On a miss, the application fetches from the database, populates the cache, and then returns the result. Writes typically go to the database and the application invalidates or updates the cache. The benefits are simplicity and memory efficiency: only frequently requested items are cached. Drawbacks include higher latency on cache misses and the danger of stale reads if invalidation is missed. A concrete example is serving user profiles: the first request loads from the database and caches the result, subsequent requests read the cache. The chapter includes starter Python code using a dictionary to simulate Redis; the implementation checks for the key, prints cache hit or miss, fetches from the database on miss, and invalidates the cache on updates. Misconception to avoid: Cache-Aside is not self-healing — your application must enforce invalidation after writes. Practice: implement the provided functions and run the test sequence to observe hits, misses, and invalidation behavior.

keyIdea.title: Cache-Aside in short
keyIdea.text: Application checks cache first, fetches from DB on miss, and is responsible for cache population and invalidation.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.6 › Cache-Aside
Pattern

Cache-Aside (Lazy Loading)

App checks cache; on miss fetch from DB, then populate cache. Writes update DB and invalidate cache.

Pros
  • Simple to implement
  • Only hot data is cached
Cons
  • Cache miss latency (two round trips)
  • Stale data unless invalidated correctly
Example

First read for a user profile is a miss and populates cache; subsequent reads are hits until an update invalidates the key.

Code (simulated)
# Simulated Cache-Aside implementation
cache = {} # In reality, a Redis/Memcached client
database = {}

def get_user_data(user_id):
  # 1. Check cache
  if user_id in cache:
    print(f"Cache hit for user {user_id}")
    return cache[user_id]

  # 2. Cache miss, fetch from database
  print(f"Cache miss for user {user_id}, fetching from DB...")
  data = database.get(user_id)

  if data:
    # 3. Store in cache
    cache[user_id] = data
    print(f"Stored user {user_id} in cache.")
  return data

def update_user_data(user_id, new_data):
  # 1. Write to database
  database[user_id] = new_data
  print(f"Updated user {user_id} in DB.")

  # 2. Invalidate cache entry
  if user_id in cache:
    del cache[user_id]
    print(f"Invalidated user {user_id} in cache.")
Run this sequence to see cache hits, misses, and invalidation behavior. Replace dictionary with Redis client in production.

screens.title: Cache-Aside: operational details and pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: Operationally, Cache-Aside hands responsibility for correctness and population to the application. On a cache miss, the app experiences higher latency because it must query the database and then insert into the cache. That extra step is acceptable when misses are rare, but becomes costly if hit rates are low. Invalidating or updating the cache after writes is critical: failing to remove or update entries leads to stale reads. One common variant is to update the database and then explicitly delete the cached entry so the next read repopulates the cache with fresh data. Mistakes to avoid include over-caching rarely used data, which increases memory costs, and relying on TTL alone when data updates must be visible immediately. Another operational risk is cache-aside-induced stampede: if an item expires and many requests miss simultaneously, they can overwhelm the database. Strategies to reduce this include single-flight locking, probabilistic TTL jitter, or pre-fetching hot items. In short, Cache-Aside is simple and efficient for read-heavy workloads but requires careful invalidation and stampede defenses. Cache-Aside: operational details and pitfalls means cache-aside is simple but shifts invalidation and stampede mitigation responsibility to the application; plan for these risks.. In practical terms, miss handling, invalidation, and common pitfalls like stale data. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.6 › Cache-Aside details
Process Flow
  1. On read: check cache → if hit return result.
  2. On miss: fetch from DB → populate cache → return result.
  3. On write: update DB → invalidate or update cache entry.
Common Pitfalls
  • Relying only on TTL for freshness when immediate consistency is required.
  • Over-caching low-value data and increasing memory costs.
  • Cache stampede when popular keys expire simultaneously.
Mitigations
Single-flight locking
Allow one request to populate cache while others wait, preventing many DB hits.
Probabilistic TTL / Jitter
Add small random offsets to TTLs to avoid synchronized expirations.
Pre-fetching
Refresh hot items before they expire using background tasks.
Reflection: when your cache miss latency is high, consider moving hot reads into the cache proactively or adding single-flight logic to avoid DB spikes.

screens.title: Write-Through vs Write-Back
screens.narratorSegment: Write-Through and Write-Back are two contrasting approaches to handling writes when a cache is present. In Write-Through, writes go to the cache and the cache synchronously persists the update to the database before confirming success to the application. This ensures the cache and database are consistent at the cost of slower writes. It's appropriate when consistency is critical and write throughput is moderate. Write-Back, sometimes called write-behind, accepts writes into the cache and returns immediately to the application, deferring the durable write to the database asynchronously. This offers very fast write latency and high throughput but introduces risk: if the cache node fails before flushing to the database, data can be lost. Use Write-Back when write throughput matters more than immediate durability, such as in logging or analytics where data can be reconstructed or slight loss is acceptable. A key misconception is that Write-Back is always preferable for performance — its operational complexity and risk often outweigh the gains unless you build robust persistence and failure recovery. Choose based on durability needs and write volume. Write-Through vs Write-Back means write-through favors consistency with slower writes; write-back favors write speed with durability risk and added complexity.. In practical terms, synchronous vs asynchronous write strategies and trade-offs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.6 › Write Strategies
Write-Through
Synchronous writes to cache and database

Writes wait for cache and DB persistence, ensuring consistency between layers at the cost of write latency.

Pros
  • Cache remains consistent with DB
  • Predictable read-after-write behavior
Cons
  • Slower writes due to synchronous DB persistence
Write-Back
Asynchronous writes from cache to database

Writes return immediately after updating cache; the cache flushes to the DB later. This maximizes write performance but risks data loss on failure.

Pros
  • Very fast write acknowledgement
  • High write throughput
Cons
  • Risk of data loss if cache fails before persistence
  • Higher implementation complexity for durability guarantees
Quick decision guide: pick Write-Through if immediate consistency is required; pick Write-Back if write throughput is the dominant requirement and some data loss is acceptable.

screens.title: Cache Invalidation Techniques
screens.narratorSegment: Cache invalidation is the process of removing or marking cached data as stale so fresh data can be served. Common techniques include time-to-live (TTL), where entries expire after a set duration; explicit invalidation, where the application deletes or updates entries after a write; publish/subscribe, where database changes emit events that cache listeners use to invalidate keys; and stale-while-revalidate, where stale data is served immediately while a background refresh obtains fresh data. TTL is simple but can serve stale data until expiration. Explicit invalidation gives precise control but requires the application to remember every key that might be affected by a write. Publish/subscribe decouples the database from cache invalidation by broadcasting updates, which is powerful in distributed systems but requires reliable eventing. Stale-while-revalidate balances performance and freshness by providing immediate responses while ensuring eventual consistency. When designing invalidation, think about how quickly users must see updates and whether slightly stale reads are acceptable. Also consider the complexity overhead: more precise invalidation requires more operational discipline. Cache Invalidation Techniques means use ttl for simplicity, explicit invalidation for correctness, pub/sub for distributed scale, and stale-while-revalidate to balance immediacy and freshness.. In practical terms, ttl, explicit invalidation, publish/subscribe, and stale-while-revalidate. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.6 › Invalidation Techniques

TTL (Time-to-Live)

Entries expire automatically after a duration. Simple to implement but can cause stale reads until expiry.

Explicit invalidation

Application removes or updates cache entries after writes to ensure freshness immediately.

Pub/Sub & Stale-While-Revalidate

Publish database changes so cache listeners can invalidate affected keys. Stale-while-revalidate serves stale data while asynchronously refreshing the cache.

Design tip: combine techniques. Use TTL for simple items, explicit invalidation for transactional updates, and pub/sub for wide-distribution systems to keep caches in sync.
Why it matters

Invalidation policy determines how fresh your reads are and how much load you place on the database; choose policies that match consistency and scale needs.

screens.title: Eviction Policies: LRU, LFU, FIFO, Random
screens.narratorSegment: When a cache reaches capacity, an eviction policy decides which items to remove. LRU, or Least Recently Used, evicts items that haven't been accessed for the longest time and works well for workloads where recent popularity predicts future access — for example, trending articles. LFU, or Least Frequently Used, evicts items accessed least often and helps when access frequency over time matters. FIFO evicts the oldest inserted items and is very simple but ignores access patterns. Random eviction chooses items at random and can be useful in systems where maintaining usage metadata is expensive. Selecting an eviction policy depends on access patterns and the workload's temporal locality. For a news site with hot trending articles, LRU is often best. For a cache of popular static lookups that remain popular over time, LFU can keep those items. A common mistake is to rely on a default eviction policy without measuring hit rates; empirical data on access frequency and recency should guide your choice. Also monitor memory usage and hit/miss ratios to validate the selected policy. Eviction Policies: LRU, LFU, FIFO, Random means pick eviction based on access patterns: lru for recent popularity, lfu for long-term popularity, fifo or random for simple or constrained systems.. Module 4 › Chapter 4.6 › Eviction Policies
LRU (Least Recently Used)

Evicts the least recently accessed item. Works well for workloads where recent access predicts near-future access, such as trending content.

LFU (Least Frequently Used)

Evicts items with the fewest accesses. Useful when long-term popularity matters.

FIFO & Random

FIFO evicts oldest items by insertion time. Random eviction is simple and avoids maintaining heavy metadata but is less optimal for hit rate.

Measure hit rate and access patterns before choosing. Many caches allow you to instrument and switch policies based on observed performance.

screens.title: Common mistakes and operational safety
screens.narratorSegment: Caching can improve performance, but certain mistakes cause outages or incorrect behavior. Over-caching everything without measuring hit rate wastes memory and increases cost without meaningful latency gains. Stale data is the most frequent correctness problem: if you fail to invalidate or use appropriate TTLs, users may see outdated information. Cache stampede, or the thundering herd, happens when a popular cached item expires and many clients simultaneously request it, causing a spike of database queries. Mitigate stampedes with locking (single-flight), pre-fetching popular items before expiry, probabilistic TTL with jitter, or stale-while-revalidate. Another danger is making the cache a single point of failure; distributed caches with replicas or consistent hashing help maintain availability. Finally, caching adds complexity: debugging stale reads, coordinating invalidation across services, and ensuring durability in write-behind setups all require operational plans and monitoring. Plan for observability: track hit/miss rates, eviction counts, and latency to detect when caching behavior diverges from expectations. Common mistakes and operational safety means avoid over-caching, enforce invalidation, protect against stampedes, and design the cache layer for high availability and observability.. screens.title: Distributed caches: Redis and Memcached
screens.narratorSegment: Distributed caches like Redis and Memcached provide a shared, in-memory key-value store that multiple application servers can access. They are optimized for very fast reads and writes, making them suitable for hot data and session storage. Redis offers features beyond simple key-value storage — data structures, persistence options, and pub/sub — while Memcached is a simpler in-memory store focused on speed. When using distributed caches you must design for availability and partitioning: clustering, replication, or consistent hashing avoid single points of failure and allow the cache to scale horizontally. Also plan for cache warm-up and rebalancing, because when nodes join or leave the cluster, the distribution of keys changes. Typical use cases include storing user session state, caching computed results, and maintaining hot lookups that would otherwise query a slow database. Remember to instrument your cache: measure latency, hit rate, and eviction activity. Choosing a distributed cache is a balance between feature needs, operational complexity, and the workload’s performance requirements. screens.title: Design decision: choosing a strategy
screens.narratorSegment: Use a decision framework when asked to pick a caching strategy. First, determine read/write ratios: for extremely read-heavy and infrequently updated content, Cache-Aside is often the best because it caches only what's needed and avoids unnecessary writes to cache. Second, assess consistency requirements: if reads must reflect recent writes immediately, Write-Through ensures cache and database stay consistent. Third, consider write volume and durability: if write throughput is the dominating metric and occasional loss is acceptable, Write-Back can dramatically increase throughput at the cost of durability and complexity. Fourth, think about operational costs: Write-Through increases write latency and DB write load, Write-Back requires robust flush and recovery logic. Finally, pick an eviction policy that matches access patterns, and design invalidation and stampede mitigations. For a news website with trending articles, Cache-Aside plus LRU is recommended. For a logging pipeline where maximum write throughput is critical and occasional loss is tolerable, Write-Back may be appropriate. When you explain your choice, always justify it in terms of read/write profile, volatility, and consistency tolerance. fullNarratorScript:
Caching is a practical, high-impact technique that reduces latency and lightens the load on databases. In real systems we place caches at multiple layers — in the client, at CDNs for static assets, in proxy layers, inside application processes, or as a distributed cache like Redis that many servers share. During this lesson you will learn the three core strategies — Cache-Aside, Write-Through, and Write-Back — and why each fits different read/write patterns. You will also learn how invalidation, TTL, and eviction policies like LRU change behavior under load. Concrete examples include using Cache-Aside for read-heavy content such as trending articles, and choosing Write-Back for very high write throughput where occasional data loss is tolerable. We will also discuss operational risks: stale data, over-caching, cache stampedes, and how to avoid single points of failure. By the end you will be able to pick a strategy, explain its trade-offs, and sketch a simple Cache-Aside implementation that uses a dictionary to simulate Redis. Think about a feature you recently used that felt slow — caching is often the fastest path to making that interaction feel instant.

By the end of these materials you will be able to explain why caching matters for latency and database load, identify where caches are commonly placed in a modern architecture, and choose a caching strategy that matches an application's read/write profile. You will also be able to describe cache invalidation techniques — TTL, explicit invalidation, and publish/subscribe — and select appropriate eviction policies like LRU or LFU based on access patterns. Finally, you'll design a simple caching layer for a backend service, implement a Cache-Aside pattern in a simulated Python environment, and reason about trade-offs such as consistency risks and cache stampedes. Each objective includes a short practical milestone so you can verify competence: implement the simulated Cache-Aside functions and answer design questions about a news site or a logging pipeline. These skills are crucial for real-world system design because caching decisions directly affect latency, cost, and consistency for high-traffic services.

These objectives map to practical tasks you can complete to show mastery. First, implement the Cache-Aside pattern using a simulated cache and database; you will verify hits and misses and perform cache invalidation after writes. Second, choose an eviction policy and explain why LRU or LFU suits your workload; practice by explaining this choice for a news or analytics service. Third, design a mitigation for cache stampede: implement a locking or stale-while-revalidate approach in your design notes and reason about trade-offs. Fourth, evaluate consistency needs and pick between Write-Through and Write-Back based on whether read performance or write durability is the priority. Each milestone is small but strategic: they force you to balance latency, cost, and correctness. As you work, keep an eye on operational complexity — caching adds speed but also a layer that must be monitored and debugged.

Caching is the practice of storing copies of data in a faster, temporary layer that sits between an application and its primary data store. The main goals are to reduce latency for frequent requests and to offload the database so the system can serve more traffic. A clear example is a user profile service: rather than hitting the slow database for every profile view, a cache stores the profile so subsequent reads are immediate. This reduces response time and decreases the number of expensive database queries. A common misconception is that caches are only for reads: while reads benefit most, writes are also important because they create stale cache entries unless invalidated. Another misconception is that caching always saves money; over-caching can increase memory costs and operational complexity without proportional benefit. Practically, you should cache only data with high access frequency or high cost to compute. When designing a cache, consider where it lives — client, CDN, proxy, in-process, or distributed — because placement affects latency, hit rate, and complexity. A good design balances speed, cost, and correctness: choose what to cache, how to invalidate it, and how to evict items when memory is full. Reflect: which part of your system would benefit most from a cache and why?

Caches appear at many levels in a system and each placement changes the trade-offs you face. Client-side caches reduce network traffic and accelerate UI interactions but are limited in size and consistency control. CDNs cache static assets like images and scripts close to users and offer strong latency benefits for geographically distributed traffic. Proxy caches can store HTTP responses at intermediate layers, reducing load on origin servers. Application-level caches live inside the server process and provide ultra-low latency, but they are local to a single instance and not shared. Distributed caches, such as Redis or Memcached, provide a shared in-memory key-value store accessible by many application servers and are the most common in backend system design; they balance speed and shareability but require careful replication and availability planning. Databases may also expose internal caches. Choosing placement depends on access locality, consistency needs, and operational constraints. For example, session state might be stored in a distributed cache to allow horizontal scaling of app servers, while static site assets belong on a CDN. A common mistake is assuming a single cache layer solves all problems — in reality you often combine several placements to meet latency and consistency goals.

Cache-Aside, also called lazy loading, is a straightforward pattern where the application checks the cache before going to the database. On a hit, the cached data is returned immediately. On a miss, the application fetches from the database, populates the cache, and then returns the result. Writes typically go to the database and the application invalidates or updates the cache. The benefits are simplicity and memory efficiency: only frequently requested items are cached. Drawbacks include higher latency on cache misses and the danger of stale reads if invalidation is missed. A concrete example is serving user profiles: the first request loads from the database and caches the result, subsequent requests read the cache. The chapter includes starter Python code using a dictionary to simulate Redis; the implementation checks for the key, prints cache hit or miss, fetches from the database on miss, and invalidates the cache on updates. Misconception to avoid: Cache-Aside is not self-healing — your application must enforce invalidation after writes. Operationally, Cache-Aside hands responsibility for correctness and population to the application. On a cache miss, the app experiences higher latency because it must query the database and then insert into the cache. That extra step is acceptable when misses are rare, but becomes costly if hit rates are low. Invalidating or updating the cache after writes is critical: failing to remove or update entries leads to stale reads. One common variant is to update the database and then explicitly delete the cached entry so the next read repopulates the cache with fresh data. Mistakes to avoid include over-caching rarely used data, which increases memory costs, and relying on TTL alone when data updates must be visible immediately. Another operational risk is cache-aside-induced stampede: if an item expires and many requests miss simultaneously, they can overwhelm the database. Strategies to reduce this include single-flight locking, probabilistic TTL jitter, or pre-fetching hot items. In short, Cache-Aside is simple and efficient for read-heavy workloads but requires careful invalidation and stampede defenses. Write-Through and Write-Back are two contrasting approaches to handling writes when a cache is present. In Write-Through, writes go to the cache and the cache synchronously persists the update to the database before confirming success to the application. This ensures the cache and database are consistent at the cost of slower writes. It's appropriate when consistency is critical and write throughput is moderate. Write-Back, sometimes called write-behind, accepts writes into the cache and returns immediately to the application, deferring the durable write to the database asynchronously. This offers very fast write latency and high throughput but introduces risk: if the cache node fails before flushing to the database, data can be lost. Use Write-Back when write throughput matters more than immediate durability, such as in logging or analytics where data can be reconstructed or slight loss is acceptable. A key misconception is that Write-Back is always preferable for performance — its operational complexity and risk often outweigh the gains unless you build robust persistence and failure recovery. Choose based on durability needs and write volume. Cache invalidation is the process of removing or marking cached data as stale so fresh data can be served. Common techniques include time-to-live (TTL), where entries expire after a set duration; explicit invalidation, where the application deletes or updates entries after a write; publish/subscribe, where database changes emit events that cache listeners use to invalidate keys; and stale-while-revalidate, where stale data is served immediately while a background refresh obtains fresh data. TTL is simple but can serve stale data until expiration. Explicit invalidation gives precise control but requires the application to remember every key that might be affected by a write. Publish/subscribe decouples the database from cache invalidation by broadcasting updates, which is powerful in distributed systems but requires reliable eventing. Stale-while-revalidate balances performance and freshness by providing immediate responses while ensuring eventual consistency. When designing invalidation, think about how quickly users must see updates and whether slightly stale reads are acceptable. Also consider the complexity overhead: more precise invalidation requires more operational discipline. When a cache reaches capacity, an eviction policy decides which items to remove. LRU, or Least Recently Used, evicts items that haven't been accessed for the longest time and works well for workloads where recent popularity predicts future access — for example, trending articles. LFU, or Least Frequently Used, evicts items accessed least often and helps when access frequency over time matters. FIFO evicts the oldest inserted items and is very simple but ignores access patterns. Random eviction chooses items at random and can be useful in systems where maintaining usage metadata is expensive. Selecting an eviction policy depends on access patterns and the workload's temporal locality. For a news site with hot trending articles, LRU is often best. For a cache of popular static lookups that remain popular over time, LFU can keep those items. A common mistake is to rely on a default eviction policy without measuring hit rates; empirical data on access frequency and recency should guide your choice. Also monitor memory usage and hit/miss ratios to validate the selected policy. Caching can improve performance, but certain mistakes cause outages or incorrect behavior. Over-caching everything without measuring hit rate wastes memory and increases cost without meaningful latency gains. Stale data is the most frequent correctness problem: if you fail to invalidate or use appropriate TTLs, users may see outdated information. Cache stampede, or the thundering herd, happens when a popular cached item expires and many clients simultaneously request it, causing a spike of database queries. Mitigate stampedes with locking (single-flight), pre-fetching popular items before expiry, probabilistic TTL with jitter, or stale-while-revalidate. Another danger is making the cache a single point of failure; distributed caches with replicas or consistent hashing help maintain availability. Finally, caching adds complexity: debugging stale reads, coordinating invalidation across services, and ensuring durability in write-behind setups all require operational plans and monitoring. Plan for observability: track hit/miss rates, eviction counts, and latency to detect when caching behavior diverges from expectations. Distributed caches like Redis and Memcached provide a shared, in-memory key-value store that multiple application servers can access. They are optimized for very fast reads and writes, making them suitable for hot data and session storage. Redis offers features beyond simple key-value storage — data structures, persistence options, and pub/sub — while Memcached is a simpler in-memory store focused on speed. When using distributed caches you must design for availability and partitioning: clustering, replication, or consistent hashing avoid single points of failure and allow the cache to scale horizontally. Also plan for cache warm-up and rebalancing, because when nodes join or leave the cluster, the distribution of keys changes. Typical use cases include storing user session state, caching computed results, and maintaining hot lookups that would otherwise query a slow database. Remember to instrument your cache: measure latency, hit rate, and eviction activity. Choosing a distributed cache is a balance between feature needs, operational complexity, and the workload’s performance requirements. Use a decision framework when asked to pick a caching strategy. First, determine read/write ratios: for extremely read-heavy and infrequently updated content, Cache-Aside is often the best because it caches only what's needed and avoids unnecessary writes to cache. Second, assess consistency requirements: if reads must reflect recent writes immediately, Write-Through ensures cache and database stay consistent. Third, consider write volume and durability: if write throughput is the dominating metric and occasional loss is acceptable, Write-Back can dramatically increase throughput at the cost of durability and complexity. Fourth, think about operational costs: Write-Through increases write latency and DB write load, Write-Back requires robust flush and recovery logic. Finally, pick an eviction policy that matches access patterns, and design invalidation and stampede mitigations. For a news website with trending articles, Cache-Aside plus LRU is recommended. For a logging pipeline where maximum write throughput is critical and occasional loss is tolerable, Write-Back may be appropriate. When you explain your choice, always justify it in terms of read/write profile, volatility, and consistency tolerance. Here are the core concepts to carry forward. First, caching stores frequently accessed data in fast temporary storage to reduce latency and database load. Second, choose a write strategy based on consistency and throughput: Cache-Aside for read-heavy workloads, Write-Through for strong consistency, and Write-Back for high write throughput with risk. Third, invalidation and eviction determine correctness and efficiency: TTL, explicit invalidation, and pub/sub keep data fresh while LRU and LFU manage limited memory. Keep these ideas in mind when designing systems and use measurements — hit rate, miss latency, and eviction counts — to validate your choices.
